title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: How should the 50% / 17% / 75% procurement figures be used `[V]`?
options: As a benchmark to show executives how far behind the organization is
For direction rather than magnitude — they come from a vendor selling bias auditing, reporting on its own audit book
They should not be used at all, since vendor research is unreliable
As evidence that pre-purchase evaluation is now a legal expectation
questions.explanation: Not false — a claim with an interest attached. A module teaching you to interrogate vendor evidence cannot quote vendor evidence uncritically, and you cannot show the sample or the question wording to an executive.

questions.prompt: Why is "what does it optimize?" the more revealing of the training questions?
options: Because vendors are reluctant to answer it

Because a model optimizing for candidates similar to current high performers has an explicit objective of reproducing your workforce's existing composition — a design decision you may not be able to defend
Because the optimization target determines the model's accuracy
Because it identifies whether the model uses protected characteristics
questions.explanation: And vendors usually answer it happily, because they are proud of it. The answer tells you what the tool is *for*, which is often not what the fairness discussion assumes.

questions.prompt: Why ask about rejected candidates' data as a data question rather than a fairness question?
options: Because data teams answer more precisely than sales teams

Because the fairness answer will not surface it — and if the system assembles information from beyond what the candidate submitted, you may be in consumer-report territory regardless of whether the model is fair
Because retention periods are contractually negotiable
Because privacy regulators enforce more aggressively than employment regulators
questions.explanation: This is the *Kistler* question. That case doesn't allege the algorithm was biased — it alleges an FCRA disclosure failure, which is a liability route that runs entirely around fairness.

questions.prompt: What makes "what would we need from you if we were sued?" worth asking before signature?
options: It signals to the vendor that you are a sophisticated buyer
Because before signature it is a procurement term, and after signature it is a request that depends on goodwill
Because it establishes the vendor's litigation history
Because it is required under most state AEDT regimes
questions.explanation: Can they produce the model version in effect on a given date, the configuration you ran, and the contemporaneous audit? That is either written into the contract or it isn't.

options: That a specific AI model has been tested for bias and passed
That an organization has an AI management system — governance, roles, controls, review — rather than that any particular model is fair
Compliance with the EU AI Act
That the vendor's training data is representative
questions.explanation: It is a management system standard, not a technical specification for an individual system. Legitimate evidence — of something other than what a fairness question asked.

questions.prompt: A vendor answers your fairness question by citing its ISO/IEC 42001 certification. What has happened?
options: Deliberate deception that should end the procurement
A subject change, usually unintentional — a salesperson asked "is it fair?" reached for the most rigorous evidence available, and it is rigorous evidence of something else
An adequate answer, since certification implies fairness testing
A legal misrepresentation
questions.explanation: Which is why naming what each document is matters: it lets you re-ask without accusing anyone of anything, and re-asking is the whole move.

questions.prompt: Which finding in an audit summary is worth *more* than a clean result?
options: A large sample size across multiple customer deployments
An audit conducted by a Big Four firm
An audit that found something and produced a change — it demonstrates the finding-to-action pathway
An audit covering every protected characteristic
questions.explanation: It shows the vendor's response-to-results mechanism works, which is the criterion Connecticut weighs and the thing Module 3's protocol is built around. A clean audit demonstrates nothing about what happens when it isn't clean.

questions.prompt: What is the sharpest argument *against* this module's gate?
options: That procurement teams lack the expertise to evaluate fairness claims
That the disparity is a property of the deployment — your pool, your job, your configuration — not of the tool, so no pre-purchase audit can establish it and the real work is all post-deployment
That vendors will refuse to answer these questions
That contract terms cannot bind model behaviour
questions.explanation: It has real force, and the weaker version of the counter is also worth holding: demanding model-level outcome evidence at the gate filters for vendors with large compliance budgets rather than for good products, which is why the activity asks for a proportionality line.
